transcript.content: Hello, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. [Name], it's... it's a long story, but I guess the short of it is that I just don't feel like myself anymore, you know? I mean, I used to be able to at least get through the day, talk to the guys on the night shift, maybe shoot the breeze about the game or whatever, but lately... lately I just barely talk to anyone. I don't even want to. It's like my whole personality has just gone flat, just totally quiet. My sister noticed it first, she said I was acting like a zombie, just staring at the wall when she came over for Sunday dinner, which I didn't even cook, by the way, I just ordered a pizza because I couldn't muster the energy to stand at the stove. And work... I've been a janitor at the community college for fifteen years, and I know that building like the back of my hand, but lately, even just getting started on my cleaning route feels like... like I'm pushing a loaded supply cart uphill in the mud. I just stand there looking at the mop bucket and I can't even figure out how to make my arms move to pick it up. It's just this heavy, empty feeling all the time, and I don't know where the old me went, but he's definitely not here right now.
How long have you been feeling this way—weeks, or has this low, flat feeling been going on for months or longer?

Weeks? No, no, it's been much longer than weeks. If I really sit down and trace it back... it’s been building for, gosh, about a year and five months now. I know the exact timeline because that’s right when everything in my life got uprooted. I had to leave my old apartment, you see. I was in that building for a long time, knew all the quirks of the radiators, knew the neighbors, the whole neighborhood really. It was my home. I had my routine down to a science—where I'd get my coffee before my evening shifts at the college, who I'd wave to on the walk to the bus stop. 

But the landlord sold the place, the rent got hiked up by the new management company, and I just couldn't swing it anymore on my salary. So I had to pack up everything I owned. Moving is hard enough, but doing it when you don't want to, when you're being forced out of the only place you feel comfortable... it just takes something out of you. And ever since I handed over those keys and left that neighborhood, right around a year and five months ago, this... this heaviness just started creeping in. At first, I figured I was just worn out from the physical labor of moving all those boxes by myself, but the exhaustion never went away. It just settled into my bones and turned into this flat, empty feeling that’s been dragging me down every single day since.
Over these past 17 months, has this low, flat feeling been present essentially every day without a break, or have there been stretches—days or weeks—where you felt more like your old self again?

Well, see, that's the strange part. It hasn't been completely solid, not exactly. I mean, mostly, yes, mostly it's just this endless, heavy slog. But... I want to say, maybe a few months back, there was this stretch. It lasted for a few weeks, maybe three or four weeks, where the fog sort of... lifted a little bit. I wouldn't say I was completely my old self, but I was getting through things better. I was actually eating the meals my sister brought over instead of just staring at them until they got cold, and I was getting through my cleaning route at the college without feeling like I was wearing lead boots. I remember I even whistled a bit while I was mopping the second-floor corridor, which I hadn't done in forever. 

But the thing is, even though I felt a bit lighter, a bit more energetic, the other stuff... the other stuff didn't stop. Even when my mood was better, I still... I still heard it. I'd be in the stairwell—the north stairwell, the one that echoes really badly—and I'd hear my name being whispered. Just... "Arthur... Arthur..." clear as day, even when I knew for a fact the building was empty. And the cameras. The security cameras in the hallways. Even when I was feeling okay, I couldn't shake the fact that they weren't just for security. I knew they were tracking me. I could feel them following my movements, recording exactly how long I spent in each room, like someone was keeping a special file just on me. So, the heaviness took a break for a few weeks, but that... that feeling of being watched, and the whispers... that never went away at all.

Thinking back, did you first start hearing your name whispered or feeling watched by the cameras around the same time your mood and energy first became low, or did those experiences start separately—either before or after that heaviness began?

Well, no, they didn't start at the exact same time, actually. It's funny you ask that, because I've thought about the timeline a lot, trying to make sense of it all in my head. Like I said, the heaviness, that terrible flat feeling, that started right around the time I had to move, about a year and five months ago. But the whispers... the whispers and the cameras... that didn't happen right away. I'd say I was in the new place, just sort of trudging through my days, for about six months before that started. 

So, if I do the math... yeah, the voices and the worries about being watched, that's been going on for about 11 months now. I remember it clearly because it was right around the time the college switched over to the winter heating schedule. I was down in the basement boiler room, just checking the gauges like I always do, and I heard it for the first time. "Arthur." Just like that. I thought it was one of the maintenance guys, maybe Dave or Luis, playing a trick on me, but I searched the whole basement and there wasn't a soul down there. And then, a few days later, I was dusting the lenses on the security cameras in the main lobby—they get this film on them from the floor wax we use—and I just got this sudden, absolute certainty that the red light on the camera wasn't just indicating it was on, but that it was actively focusing on me. Not just the lobby, but me specifically. So, yeah, the low mood came first, and then about six months later, 11 months ago, the other stuff started. And like I said, even when the heavy feeling lifted for those few weeks, the cameras and the whispers... they just kept right on going. They haven't stopped at all for these past 11 months.

Aside from these low periods, have you ever had stretches—even just a few days—where you felt unusually energetic, elated, or 'on top of the world,' needed much less sleep than usual, or felt like your thoughts were racing?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I've never been the type to bounce off the walls or feel like I could take on the world, you know? Even before all this started, back when I was in my old apartment and things were just... normal. I was always just a steady guy. I liked my routine. Wake up, make my coffee—French roast, usually, with just a splash of milk—read the paper, go to my shift. I never had these bursts of energy where I didn't need to sleep. Sleep is... well, sleep has always been important to me. If I don't get my seven hours, I'm just dragging the buffer across the cafeteria floor the next day. 

And racing thoughts? No, my mind doesn't race. If anything, it just gets stuck. Like a record skipping on the same groove. Especially lately, with the cameras and the whispers, my thoughts just circle around those same things. But it's not fast, it's not like a million ideas at once. It's just... heavy. Plodding. Even during that brief stretch I told you about, where the fog lifted a bit and I was whistling in the hallway... I wasn't elated. I wasn't on top of the world. I was just... okay. Just functioning like a regular person again for a minute. I was just glad to not feel like I was walking through molasses. But I never had a time where I felt unusually high or energetic. Just... just the low, and then the brief bit of okay, and the voices. That's all.

Doctor, you didn't ask a question just now. You just... well, you just stopped. I mean, I'm sitting here, and I just finished telling you about how I never get those high, energetic moods, how I'm just a steady guy who likes his French roast and his routine, and then... nothing. You're just looking at me. 

Did you... did you want me to elaborate more on that? Because I can tell you more about how my mind works when it gets stuck, if that's what you're waiting for. Like I said, it's like a record skipping. I'll be in the supply closet on the third floor—the one where we keep the heavy-duty floor wax and the extra mop heads—and I'll just stand there holding a bottle of cleaner, and my brain will just loop over and over about the cameras. "Are they watching the closet door? Did they see me come in? How long have I been in here? Are they timing me?" It just goes round and round, slow and heavy, not fast at all. 

Or did you mean something else? I'm not really sure what you want me to say next if you don't ask me anything. I want to be helpful, I really do. My sister told me it was important to be completely honest and thorough with you, so I'm trying to give you all the details you need to figure out what's going on with me, with the whispers and the flat feeling and everything. But you have to tell me what you need to know. What are you thinking about right now? What's the next question?

Sorry, Doctor, you didn't ask a question just now. You just... well, you just stopped talking. I mean, I'm sitting here, and I just finished telling you about how my mind works, how I'm just a steady guy who likes his French roast and his routine, and then... nothing. You're just looking at me. 

Did you... did you want me to elaborate more on that? Because I can tell you more about how my mind works when it gets stuck, if that's what you're waiting for. Like I said, it's like a record skipping. I'll be in the supply closet on the third floor—the one where we keep the heavy-duty floor wax and the extra mop heads, you know the type of closet I mean, usually smells like pine and bleach—and I'll just stand there holding a bottle of cleaner, and my brain will just loop over and over about the cameras. "Are they watching the closet door? Did they see me come in? How long have I been in here? Are they timing me?" It just goes round and round, slow and heavy, not fast at all. 

Or did you mean something else? I'm not really sure what you want me to say next if you don't ask me anything. I want to be helpful, I really do. My sister told me it was important to be completely honest and thorough with you, so I'm trying to give you all the details you need to figure out what's going on with me, with the whispers and the flat feeling and everything. But you have to tell me what you need to know. What are you thinking about right now? What's the next question?
